title: Twenty-Seven Dollars in Jobra

lines.say: Forty-two villagers owed twenty-seven dollars between them.

lines.text: What one professor did about it would spread to almost every country.
Muhammad Yunus taught economics in Bangladesh, during a terrible famine.
lines.say: Moo-hah-mad Yoo-nuss taught economics in Bangladesh, during a terrible famine.

lines.text: In Jobra, a woman borrowed less than a dollar from a moneylender.
lines.say: In Job-rah, a woman borrowed less than a dollar from a moneylender.

lines.text: Only he could buy what she made, at a price he set.
Yunus offered the twenty-seven dollars from his own pocket.
lines.say: Yoo-nuss offered the twenty-seven dollars from his own pocket.

lines.text: Then he asked the bank on his campus to lend to people like them.
The bank said 'the poor were not creditworthy.'
After months of trying, Yunus offered to guarantee the loans himself.
lines.say: After months of trying, Yoo-nuss offered to guarantee the loans himself.

lines.text: And the borrowers paid back on time, he later recalled.
Grameen Bank came to lend through groups of five neighbours.
lines.say: Grah-meen Bank came to lend through groups of five neighbours.

lines.text: If one member defaulted, the whole group lost the right to borrow again.
This is solidarity lending. Economists argued neighbours' trust did the work that collateral does.

caption: A bank said the poor were not creditworthy. Then they paid back on time. Solidarity lending puts borrowers in small groups so neighbours' trust stands in for collateral. A true story, fact-checked. Tomorrow: Self-Improvement. Curiouser No. 12
